children.text: Use a nonrelativistic Bohr hydrogen model with fixed proton, electron mass me and charge magnitude e. Orbital angular momentum is \(L=n\hbar\), n a positive integer, and \(\alpha=e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c)\simeq7.27\times10^{-3}\). Use \(\hbar\), not h, except for photon energy written as \(2\pi\hbar c/\lambda\). For numerical work use \(m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(m_p=1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(\hbar=1.055\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\), \(e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\), \(1\,\mathrm{kpc}=3.09\times10^{19}\,\mathrm m\), and \(M_\odot=1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\). Later parts study the supplied galaxy rotation, hydrogen radio and Tully-Fisher graphs. The stipulated spin moment is \(\mathcal M_s=e\hbar/m_e\), with \(\Delta E_{HF}\simeq3.72(m_e/m_p)\Delta E_F\). This is the question model, not a precision atomic calculation.
Find speed v at orbital radius r.
Show \(r_n=n^2r_1\). Find r1 in terms of alpha, me,c,hbar and evaluate it to three digits. Express v1 in terms of alpha and c.
Find En in terms of e, epsilon0,r1,n and E1 in terms of alpha,me,c. Give E1 in eV.
In the electron frame a proton orbits at radius r1 and speed v1. Find the field magnitude B1 at the electron.
Find the parallel-antiparallel splitting Delta EF in terms of alpha and E1. Then find the hyperfine photon wavelength and evaluate it to two digits.
For a spherically symmetric gravitational potential per mass phi(r), find circular speed in terms of r and dphi/dr.

Let \(\varphi_G(r,z)=\varphi_0\ln(r/r_0)\exp[-(z/z_0)^2]\), with phi0 positive and r<r0. At constant r derive the vertical motion equation and small-oscillation frequency.
For z=0 identify which radial regime of B.3 yields the logarithmic potential and find vc in terms of phi0.

statement.text:
Hydrogen and Galaxies
Use a nonrelativistic Bohr hydrogen model with fixed proton, electron mass me and charge magnitude e. Orbital angular momentum is \(L=n\hbar\), n a positive integer, and \(\alpha=e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c)\simeq7.27\times10^{-3}\). Use \(\hbar\), not h, except for photon energy written as \(2\pi\hbar c/\lambda\). For numerical work use \(m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(m_p=1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(\hbar=1.055\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\), \(e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\), \(1\,\mathrm{kpc}=3.09\times10^{19}\,\mathrm m\), and \(M_\odot=1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\). Later parts study the supplied galaxy rotation, hydrogen radio and Tully-Fisher graphs. The stipulated spin moment is \(\mathcal M_s=e\hbar/m_e\), with \(\Delta E_{HF}\simeq3.72(m_e/m_p)\Delta E_F\). This is the question model, not a precision atomic calculation.
A.1. Circular electron speed
Find speed v at orbital radius r.
A.2. Bohr orbit scales
Show \(r_n=n^2r_1\). Find r1 in terms of alpha, me,c,hbar and evaluate it to three digits. Express v1 in terms of alpha and c.
A.3. Bound-state energy
Find En in terms of e, epsilon0,r1,n and E1 in terms of alpha,me,c. Give E1 in eV.
A.4. Proton-current field
In the electron frame a proton orbits at radius r1 and speed v1. Find the field magnitude B1 at the electron.
A.5. Hyperfine emission
Find the parallel-antiparallel splitting Delta EF in terms of alpha and E1. Then find the hyperfine photon wavelength and evaluate it to two digits.
B.1. Circular galactic motion
For a spherically symmetric gravitational potential per mass phi(r), find circular speed in terms of r and dphi/dr.
B.2. Visible-bulge mass

The red curve assumes a homogeneous bulge within 1 kpc and Keplerian motion outside it. Estimate the NGC 6946 bulge mass from that curve, in solar masses.
B.3. Extended density model
Take \(\rho_m=C_m/(r_m^2+r^2)\), Cm and rm positive. Show \(v_{c,m}=\sqrt{k_1-k_2\arctan(r/r_m)/r}\), find k1,k2, and give small- and large-radius limits. Simplify enclosed mass at large r and estimate mass within the visible image. You may use \(\int_0^r x^2/(a^2+x^2)dx=r-a\arctan(r/a)\).
C.1. Vertical galactic stability
Let \(\varphi_G(r,z)=\varphi_0\ln(r/r_0)\exp[-(z/z_0)^2]\), with phi0 positive and r<r0. At constant r derive the vertical motion equation and small-oscillation frequency.
C.2. Flat rotation regime
For z=0 identify which radial regime of B.3 yields the logarithmic potential and find vc in terms of phi0.
C.3. Galactic radial velocity

The Sun is at radius RSun=8.00 kpc. A hydrogen emitter at radius R is seen at longitude ell from the Galactic centre. Both orbit at the same speed vSun. Find emitter radial velocity relative to the Sun, positive for recession, and invert for R.
C.4. Three hydrogen sources

At longitude 30 degrees and rest frequency f0=1.42 GHz, use the three radio peaks to find radial velocities to three significant digits and radii as multiples of RSun to two significant digits. Take vSun=220 km/s.
C.5. Source positions
Sketch possible positions of the three sources in the Galactic plane and explain what changing ell can reveal.
D.1. Tully-Fisher exponents

Assume galaxy radius R is independent of mass. Find gamma and eta in \(M_{tot}=\eta v_{c,\infty}^\gamma\) from B.3, then estimate the observed exponent from the logarithmic graph.
D.2. Outer-galaxy acceleration
Estimate Newtonian centripetal acceleration in the outer region of NGC 6946.
D.3. Deep-MOND scaling
MOND modifies dynamics to \(\mathbf F=m\mu(a/a_0)\mathbf a\), with \(\mu(x)=x/(1+x)\). For a circular orbit about mass M and a much less than a0, find the Tully-Fisher exponent and estimate a0 from the galaxy data.
D.4. MOND rotation curve
For mass M uniformly distributed inside radius Rb, determine vc(r) for all radii with the full interpolation function.

children.text: Balance Coulomb attraction and centripetal force: \(m_ev^2/r=e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)\), giving \(v=\sqrt{e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0m_er)}\).

Use \(m_ev_nr_n=n\hbar\) with force balance. Then \[r_n=n^2\frac\hbar{\alpha m_ec},\quad r_1\simeq5.3\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm m,\quad v_1=\alpha c.\] The precise rounded radius depends on using the supplied alpha=0.00727 or the more accurate fine-structure constant. At the supplied alpha r1 is about \(5.31\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm m\).

The potential is minus twice the kinetic energy, so \[E_n=-\frac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0r_1n^2},\qquad E_1=-\tfrac12\alpha^2m_ec^2\simeq-13.5\,\mathrm{eV}.\] Using the unrounded physical alpha gives the usual -13.6 eV.
The current is \(ev_1/(2\pi r_1)\). The circular-current field is \(\mu_0I/(2r_1)\), hence \[B_1=\mu_0e\alpha c/(4\pi r_1^2).\]

The interaction energy is \(-\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}_s\cdot\mathbf B_1\), so \(\Delta E_F=2\mathcal M_sB_1=-4\alpha^2E_1\). Use the stated hyperfine factor and \(\lambda_{HF}=2\pi\hbar c/\Delta E_{HF}\) to obtain approximately 0.21 m. The energy difference is positive although the bound-state E1 is negative.

Outside the bulge, \(M_b=v_c^2r/G\). Read approximately 20 km/s at 10 kpc from the red curve. This yields \(M_b\simeq1.85\times10^{39}\,\mathrm{kg}\simeq9.3\times10^8M_\odot\). Graph-reading precision is limited.

Spherical integration gives \[M(r)=4\pi C_m[r-r_m\arctan(r/r_m)].\] Thus \(k_1=4\pi GC_m,k_2=4\pi GC_mr_m\). At small r, \(v\simeq\sqrt{4\pi GC_m/3}\,r/r_m\). At large r, \(v\to\sqrt{4\pi GC_m}\) and \(M(r)\simeq4\pi C_mr\). The graph plateau near 160 km/s gives \(C_m\simeq3.05\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{kg/m}\). For image radius about 9 kpc the large-r estimate is \(M\simeq1.07\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{kg}\), about \(5.4\times10^{10}M_\odot\), hence order \(10^{11}M_\odot\). This substantially exceeds the visible-bulge estimate. The source converts 9 kpc incorrectly in one line; using 3.09 times 10 to the 19 metres per kpc fixes it.
\[\ddot z=\frac{2\varphi_0z}{z_0^2}\ln(r/r_0)e^{-(z/z_0)^2}.\] Since the logarithm is negative, the linear force restores z to zero and \[\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{2\varphi_0}{z_0^2}\ln(r_0/r)}.\]
At \(r\gg r_m\), \(d\varphi/dr=4\pi GC_m/r\), so \(\varphi=4\pi GC_m\ln(r/r_0)\). Identify \(\varphi_0=4\pi GC_m\), giving \(v_c=\sqrt{\varphi_0}\).
Project the two tangential velocities onto the sightline: \[v_r=v_\odot(R_\odot/R-1)\sin\ell,\qquad R=\frac{R_\odot}{1+v_r/(v_\odot\sin\ell)}.\] Longitudes with zero sine cannot determine R this way.

The peaks have shift magnitudes 0.03,0.15,0.26 MHz. Interpreting the plotted positive shift as the receding Doppler convention yields \(v_r\simeq6.33,31.7,54.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\), and \(R/R_\odot\simeq0.95,0.78,0.67\). A positive received-frequency shift f-f0 would instead mean approach. The source labels its shift inconsistently with its positive-recession velocities. These values use its intended redshift magnitude, not a silent Doppler sign reversal.

Draw the sightline at 30 degrees from Sun-to-centre, then circles of radii 0.95,0.78,0.67 RSun. Each intersects the line at near and far candidates. Repeated directions trace hydrogen structure, including spiral arms, but simple kinematics alone leaves the near-far ambiguity inside the solar circle. Brightness alone does not uniquely resolve it.

Combining \(M\simeq4\pi C_mR\) and \(v_\infty^2=4\pi GC_m\) gives gamma=2 and eta=R/G. The plotted slope is about \((12-9)/(2.6-1.8)=3.75\), near 4, rather than 2. The printed source fraction reverses numerator and denominator but its numerical value uses this correct slope.
Use \(a=v^2/r\). At v=160 km/s and r=5 kpc, \(a\simeq1.66\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), decreasing farther out.

Deep MOND gives \(a^2/a_0=GM/r^2\). With a=v squared/r, \(v_\infty^4=GMa_0\), so the exponent is 4. Reading \(M\sim10^{10.5}M_\odot\) at v=160 km/s gives \(a_0\sim1.6\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). The outer data are of this order, becoming more deeply MOND farther out. An acceleration merely comparable to a0 is a crossover rather than asymptotically much less than a0.

Let \(g_N=GMr/R_b^3\) inside and \(g_N=GM/r^2\) outside. The equation \(a^2/(a+a_0)=g_N\) has positive root \[a=\tfrac12[g_N+\sqrt{g_N^2+4a_0g_N}],\qquad v_c=\sqrt{ra}.\] This compact piecewise-gN expression covers both regions and matches continuously at Rb. At infinity it approaches \((GMa_0)^{1/4}\); at the centre it vanishes, with deep-MOND scaling \(v_c\propto r^{3/4}\).

B.1. Circular galactic motion

B.2. Visible-bulge mass
